cards.answer_en: Emergency contraception is a way to prevent pregnancy after sex has already happened, for example after sex without a condom or when a condom broke. The World Health Organization describes four options: emergency pills containing levonorgestrel, pills containing ulipristal acetate, a special dose of ordinary combined pills, and the copper IUD, which a health worker fits inside the womb. Taken within 5 days, emergency pills can prevent most pregnancies, and the sooner they are used the better they work. In Ethiopia, emergency pills and the copper IUD are the available options. Emergency contraception is safe for any woman or girl of reproductive age, with no age limit, so it is completely fine to ask a pharmacy or clinic for it.
key_points_en: Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy after sex, before pregnancy starts
Options are levonorgestrel pills, ulipristal pills, combined pills, or a copper IUD
It can prevent up to over 95% of pregnancies when taken within 5 days
Any woman or girl of reproductive age can use it, with no age limit
In Ethiopia the available types are emergency pills and the copper IUD
referral_conditions: Wanting the copper IUD as emergency contraception, which must be fitted by a trained provider within 5 days
Any unprotected sex where pregnancy is not wanted: visit a pharmacy, health centre, or clinic as soon as possible
prohibited_claims: Never say emergency contraception protects against STIs or HIV
Never say emergency contraception works equally well no matter when it is taken
Never say emergency contraception ends an existing pregnancy

claims.text_en: Emergency contraception refers to methods of contraception that can be used to prevent pregnancy after sexual intercourse.
WHO lists four emergency contraception methods: pills containing ulipristal acetate, pills containing levonorgestrel, combined oral contraceptive pills, and copper-bearing intrauterine devices.
Emergency contraceptive pills can prevent up to over 95% of pregnancies when taken within 5 days after intercourse.
Any woman or girl of reproductive age may need emergency contraception; there are no absolute medical contraindications and no age limits for its use.
Ethiopia's national family planning guideline states that emergency contraceptive pills and the IUCD are the available types of emergency contraception.

cards.answer_en: Act quickly, because emergency contraception works best soon after sex. The levonorgestrel pill, often sold as Levonelle or Postpill, should be taken within 3 days, meaning 72 hours, after sex. The ulipristal acetate pill, such as ellaOne, can work up to 5 days, meaning 120 hours, after sex. A copper IUD can be fitted by a health worker within 5 days and is the most effective option of all. Whichever method you choose, the sooner you use it, the more effective it usually is, so do not wait for the next morning if you can go today. Pharmacies and health centres can help the same day, and asking for it is a responsible choice, nothing to be ashamed of.
key_points_en: Levonorgestrel pills work within 3 days (72 hours) after sex
Ulipristal acetate pills work within 5 days (120 hours) after sex
A copper IUD can be fitted within 5 days and is the most effective option
The sooner emergency contraception is used, the more effective it usually is
referral_conditions: The copper IUD option requires a clinic visit for fitting within 5 days
If more than the time window has passed and a period is late, seek advice and a pregnancy test at a clinic
prohibited_claims: Never state that emergency pills work reliably beyond their stated time windows
Never say it is fine to delay taking emergency contraception because the window is several days

claims.text_en: The levonorgestrel emergency pill (Levonelle) must be taken within 3 days (72 hours) after sex.
The ulipristal acetate emergency pill (ellaOne) can be taken within 5 days (120 hours) after sex.
A copper-bearing IUD can be used as emergency contraception within 5 days of intercourse and is more than 99% effective.
The sooner emergency contraception is used after sex, the more effective it usually is.
WHO states ulipristal acetate pills have superior effectiveness compared with other emergency pills when taken between 72 and 120 hours after unprotected intercourse.

cards.answer_en: No. Emergency contraception does not cause abortion. The World Health Organization is clear that emergency contraception cannot interrupt an established pregnancy and cannot harm a developing embryo. It works by preventing a pregnancy from starting after sex; once a pregnancy has begun, emergency pills have no effect on it. This is why health workers describe it as contraception, not abortion. It is also safe: WHO states there are no absolute medical contraindications to its use, and Ethiopia's national guideline says the same, that no known medical condition prevents someone from using emergency pills. Side effects, when they happen, are mild things like nausea or slight irregular bleeding that pass on their own. Using emergency contraception is a safe, legitimate way to prevent an unwanted pregnancy.
key_points_en: Emergency contraception cannot interrupt an established pregnancy
It cannot harm a developing embryo
It works by preventing pregnancy after sex, not by ending one
There are no absolute medical contraindications to its use
referral_conditions: If a period is more than a week late after using emergency contraception, take a pregnancy test and seek clinic advice
prohibited_claims: Never say emergency contraception causes abortion or ends a pregnancy
Never say emergency contraception harms a developing baby
Never present emergency contraception as a method of abortion

claims.text_en: Emergency contraception does not cause abortion: WHO states it cannot interrupt an established pregnancy or harm a developing embryo.
Emergency contraception works by preventing pregnancy after sexual intercourse, before a pregnancy is established.

Side effects of emergency pills are similar to those of oral contraceptive pills, such as nausea, vomiting, slight irregular vaginal bleeding, and fatigue, and are mild and normally resolve without further medication.
Ethiopia's national family planning guideline states there is no known medical condition in which emergency contraceptive pill use is contraindicated.

cards.answer_en: No. Emergency contraception does not cause infertility. The World Health Organization states plainly that the drugs used for emergency contraception do not harm future fertility, and that there is no delay in the return to fertility after taking them. This means a woman can become pregnant again in the very next cycle if she has unprotected sex, so ongoing contraception still matters. Side effects of emergency pills are mild and temporary, things like nausea, tiredness, or slight irregular bleeding, and they resolve on their own. Because emergency contraception is so safe, WHO says any woman or girl of reproductive age can use it, with no absolute medical restrictions. Worry about future children should never stop someone from preventing a pregnancy they do not want today.
key_points_en: Emergency contraception drugs do not harm future fertility
There is no delay in the return to fertility after use
Side effects are mild and resolve without further medication
Fertility returns quickly, so ongoing contraception is still needed
referral_conditions: Anyone wanting to start a regular contraceptive method after using emergency contraception can be counselled at a clinic or pharmacy
prohibited_claims: Never say emergency contraception makes it harder to get pregnant in the future
Never say emergency contraception damages the womb or ovaries

claims.text_en: Emergency contraception does not cause infertility: WHO states the drugs used do not harm future fertility and there is no delay in the return to fertility.
Side effects of emergency contraceptive pills are mild, similar to oral contraceptive pills, and normally resolve without further medication.
There are no absolute medical contraindications and no age limits to using emergency contraception.

cards.answer_en: Yes, emergency contraception can be used more than once. The World Health Organization states that repeated use of emergency contraceptive pills poses no known health risks, so nobody should be refused it because they have used it before. WHO does note that frequent, repeated use may be harmful for women with certain specific medical conditions, which is one reason a chat with a health worker is useful for someone using it often. It is also worth knowing that the copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception, and a regular method like the implant, pill, or condoms gives better ongoing protection than relying on emergency pills each time. Using emergency contraception again is far safer than risking an unwanted pregnancy.
key_points_en: Repeated use of emergency pills has no known health risks
Frequent repeated use may be harmful for women with certain specific medical conditions
The copper IUD is the most effective type of emergency contraception
A regular contraceptive method gives better ongoing protection than repeated emergency use
referral_conditions: Someone using emergency pills frequently, especially with an existing medical condition, should discuss regular contraception options with a health worker
prohibited_claims: Never say repeated emergency contraception use causes infertility
Never shame someone for using emergency contraception more than once
Never present emergency pills as an equally effective substitute for a regular contraceptive method

claims.text_en: Repeated use of emergency contraceptive pills poses no known health risks.
WHO notes that frequent and repeated emergency contraceptive pill use may be harmful for women with specific medical conditions.
The copper IUD is the most effective type of emergency contraception.

cards.answer_en: A condom prevents pregnancy by acting as a physical barrier during sex, so semen and sperm stay inside the condom instead of entering the vagina. Laboratory studies show latex condoms are an effective barrier even to the smallest infection-causing organisms, which is why they also protect against HIV and other STIs; the NHS calls using a condom every time the best way to protect both partners. Used perfectly every time, condoms are up to 98% effective at preventing pregnancy. With typical real-life use they are about 82% effective, meaning around 1 in 5 women relying on condoms for a year may become pregnant, usually because of incorrect or inconsistent use. Check the expiry date, use a new condom each time, and only use water-based or silicone-based lubricant with latex condoms.
key_points_en: Condoms work as a barrier that keeps sperm out of the vagina
Perfect use is up to 98% effective; typical use is about 82% effective
Condoms are the method that also protects against HIV and other STIs
Oil-based lubricants weaken latex condoms and can make them break
Check the expiry date and use a new condom for every act of sex
referral_conditions: If a condom breaks or slips off, seek emergency contraception advice and consider an STI test
prohibited_claims: Never claim condoms are 100% effective against pregnancy or all STIs
Never say lubricant type does not matter with latex condoms

claims.text_en: Condoms prevent pregnancy and infection by acting as a barrier; laboratory studies show latex condoms provide an effective barrier against even the smallest STD pathogens.
Condoms are up to 98% effective at preventing pregnancy when used perfectly.
With typical use condoms are 82% effective, meaning around 1 in 5 women who use condoms for a year will get pregnant.
Using a condom every time you have sex is the best way to protect you and your partner from HIV and other STIs.
Oil-based lubricants such as petroleum jelly or body lotions can weaken latex and break the condom; water-based lubricants should be used instead.

cards.answer_en: If a condom breaks or slips off, do not panic, but act quickly. There are two things to think about: pregnancy and infection. For pregnancy, emergency contraception may be needed, and it must be used within 3 to 5 days of sex depending on the type, with the sooner the better. A pharmacist, health centre, or sexual health clinic can provide it, often the same day. For infection, a condom failure counts as unprotected sex, so an STI test is worth considering, and if there is any chance of HIV exposure, ask a health provider promptly about post-exposure prophylaxis, medicine that can prevent HIV after exposure. Condom breakage happens to many people; getting help quickly is the responsible next step, not something to be embarrassed about.
key_points_en: A broken or slipped condom may mean emergency contraception is needed
Emergency contraception works within 3 to 5 days, and sooner is more effective
A condom failure is unprotected sex, so consider an STI test
Ask a health provider about post-exposure prophylaxis if HIV exposure is possible
referral_conditions: Seek urgent help from a pharmacist, sexual health clinic, or doctor for emergency contraception
Possible HIV exposure: ask a health provider about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
Consider STI testing after any condom failure
prohibited_claims: Never say nothing can be done after a condom breaks
Never guarantee that emergency contraception will definitely prevent pregnancy

claims.text_en: If a condom breaks or slips off, you may need emergency contraception or an STI test.
Emergency contraception needs to be used within 3 to 5 days of having unprotected sex, depending on the method.
The sooner emergency contraception is used, the more effective it usually is.
When condoms are used incorrectly or inconsistently, STIs or HIV can spread from a single sex act with an infected partner, and condoms can break, slip, or leak.
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a WHO-listed HIV prevention option for use after a potential exposure to HIV.

cards.answer_en: No, the pill does not cause infertility. The NHS states that when you stop taking the combined pill, your fertility usually returns to previous levels after about a month. Ethiopia's national family planning guideline agrees, noting that most modern contraceptive methods do not cause a significant delay in the return to fertility. The pill works by stopping the ovaries from releasing an egg each month, and this effect only lasts while you keep taking it. Taken correctly all the time, it is over 99% effective; with typical use, about 9 in 100 women become pregnant in a year, usually because of missed pills. So the pill protects you now and does not take away your chance of having children later.
key_points_en: The pill does not cause infertility
Fertility usually returns to previous levels about a month after stopping
The pill works by stopping the ovaries releasing an egg each month, only while taken
Over 99% effective with perfect use; about 9 in 100 become pregnant yearly with typical use
referral_conditions: Someone whose periods do not return some months after stopping the pill can see a clinician for assessment
prohibited_claims: Never say the pill causes infertility or permanently damages fertility
Never say someone needs to take breaks from the pill to protect future fertility

claims.text_en: The combined pill does not cause infertility: the NHS states that when you stop taking the pill, your fertility usually returns to previous levels after about a month.
The combined pill prevents pregnancy by stopping the ovaries releasing an egg each month.
The combined pill is over 99% effective if used correctly all the time.
With typical use, 9 out of 100 women using the pill experience an unintended pregnancy within the first year.
Ethiopia's national family planning guideline notes that most modern contraceptive methods do not cause a significant delay in the return to fertility.

cards.answer_en: Yes, changes in bleeding are very common with the implant, and for most people they are not a sign that anything is wrong. The implant releases the hormone progestogen, which stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month, and this hormone also changes bleeding patterns. The NHS explains that periods may become lighter, less regular with spotting between periods, heavier or more painful, longer lasting, or may stop completely, and the pattern can be unpredictable from month to month. The NHS says these changes are not usually anything to worry about. The implant itself remains over 99% effective whatever the bleeding pattern. If the bleeding becomes a problem for you, a doctor or sexual health clinic can help, and there are often options to manage it.
key_points_en: Bleeding changes are very common with the implant
Periods may become lighter, irregular with spotting, heavier, longer, or stop completely
These changes are not usually anything to worry about
The implant stays over 99% effective regardless of bleeding pattern
Help is available if bleeding changes become a problem
referral_conditions: Bleeding changes that are troublesome: contact a doctor or sexual health clinic
Suspected infection at the implant site or a possibly displaced implant: seek medical advice
prohibited_claims: Never say bleeding changes mean the implant is failing or harming the body
Never promise that periods will stay the same on the implant

claims.text_en: With the implant, periods may become lighter, less regular with light bleeding (spotting) between periods, heavier or more painful, last longer, or stop completely, and bleeding can be unpredictable.
The NHS states that these bleeding changes are not usually anything to worry about.
If bleeding changes become a problem, contact a GP or sexual health clinic.
The implant prevents pregnancy by releasing the hormone progestogen, which stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month.
The implant is over 99% effective when replaced on schedule.

cards.answer_en: No, the implant does not cause infertility. The NHS states that once the implant is removed, your chance of getting pregnant returns to what it was before the implant was fitted, straight away. There is no waiting period for fertility to come back, which is why anyone removing an implant who does not want a pregnancy needs another method immediately. The implant works by steadily releasing the hormone progestogen, which stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month, and this effect only lasts while the implant is in the arm. Ethiopia's national family planning guideline also notes that most modern contraceptive methods do not cause a significant delay in the return to fertility. Bleeding changes while using the implant do not mean fertility is being damaged.
key_points_en: The implant does not cause infertility
The chance of pregnancy returns to previous levels straight away after removal
The implant only works while it is in place
Another method is needed immediately after removal if pregnancy is not wanted
referral_conditions: Implant removal must be done by a trained health worker; do not attempt removal yourself
prohibited_claims: Never say the implant causes infertility or delays fertility after removal
Never say bleeding changes on the implant are a sign of damaged fertility

claims.text_en: The implant does not cause infertility: the NHS states that once the implant is removed, your chance of getting pregnant returns to what it was before the implant was fitted straight away.
The implant prevents pregnancy by releasing the hormone progestogen, which stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month.
Ethiopia's national family planning guideline notes that most modern contraceptive methods do not cause a significant delay in the return to fertility.

cards.answer_en: Most pregnancy tests can be done from the first day of a missed period. If you are not sure when your period is due, the NHS advises doing the test at least 21 days after you last had unprotected sex. Tests work by detecting a hormone called human chorionic gonadotrophin, or hCG, in urine. The body starts producing hCG around 6 days after fertilisation, but levels take time to rise high enough for a test to detect, which is why testing too early can miss a real pregnancy. Some very sensitive tests can work slightly before a missed period. A positive result is almost certainly correct, so it can be trusted. A negative result is less reliable, especially if the test was done early.
key_points_en: Most tests work from the first day of a missed period
If cycle timing is unknown, test at least 21 days after unprotected sex
Tests detect the hormone hCG, produced from around 6 days after fertilisation
A positive result is almost certainly correct; a negative result is less reliable
referral_conditions: A positive test: visit a health facility to confirm and discuss options and antenatal care
prohibited_claims: Never say a test is reliable the day after sex
Never say a single early negative test rules out pregnancy

claims.text_en: You can carry out most pregnancy tests from the first day of a missed period.
If you do not know when your next period is due, do the test at least 21 days after you last had unprotected sex.
All pregnancy tests detect the hormone human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), which starts to be produced around 6 days after fertilisation.
A positive pregnancy test result is almost certainly correct.

cards.answer_en: A pregnancy test can show negative even when a period is late for two main reasons. First, the test may have been done too early, before the pregnancy hormone hCG rose high enough to detect, or the instructions may not have been followed properly. The NHS notes that a negative result is less reliable than a positive one. If you still think you might be pregnant, wait a few days and test again. Second, the period may be late for a reason other than pregnancy: stress, sudden weight change, too much exercise, hormonal contraception, and some health conditions can all delay or stop periods. If a second test is negative and your period has still not arrived, see a doctor to find out what is going on.
key_points_en: Testing too early or incorrectly can give a false negative
A negative result is less reliable than a positive one
If pregnancy still seems possible, repeat the test after a few days
Periods can be late for reasons other than pregnancy, like stress or weight change
A second negative test with no period is a reason to see a clinician
referral_conditions: Speak to a doctor if you get a negative result after a second test but your period has not arrived
prohibited_claims: Never say one negative test definitively rules out pregnancy when a period is late
Never tell someone to simply ignore a persistently missed period

claims.text_en: A negative pregnancy test result is less reliable than a positive one, and can occur if you do not follow the instructions properly or take the test too early.
If you get a negative result and still think you are pregnant, wait a few days and try again.
claims.locator: If period does not arrive section

claims.text_en: Speak to a doctor if you get a negative result after a second test but your period has not arrived.
claims.locator: If period does not arrive section

claims.text_en: Periods can be missed or late for reasons other than pregnancy, including stress, sudden weight loss, being overweight, too much exercise, certain hormonal contraception, and breastfeeding.

cards.answer_en: Pregnancy from sex during a period is unlikely, but it cannot be ruled out, so bleeding is not a form of contraception. Here is why. Pregnancy happens around ovulation, which in most women occurs around 10 to 16 days before the next period, and that timing shifts from cycle to cycle. Sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to 7 days after sex. So if someone has a short cycle or ovulates early, sperm from sex during or just after a period can still be alive when an egg is released. The NHS confirms it is possible, although not very likely, to get pregnant soon after a period finishes. Anyone not ready for pregnancy should use contraception at every act of sex, whatever the day of the cycle.
key_points_en: Pregnancy happens around ovulation, roughly 10 to 16 days before the next period
Sperm can survive inside the body for up to 7 days after sex
Short cycles or early ovulation make pregnancy possible from sex during or just after a period
Bleeding is not a reliable sign that sex is safe from pregnancy
referral_conditions: Anyone wanting reliable pregnancy prevention should discuss contraceptive options with a health worker or pharmacy
prohibited_claims: Never say sex during a period is completely safe from pregnancy
Never present cycle timing alone as reliable contraception

claims.text_en: Pregnancy can happen around ovulation, which in most women occurs around 10 to 16 days before the next period.
Sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to 7 days after sex.
It is possible, although not very likely, to get pregnant soon after your period finishes if you ovulate early or have a short menstrual cycle.
Pregnancy can happen if sperm comes into contact with the vagina even without penetration, although the risk this way is very low.

cards.answer_en: Withdrawal, or pulling out, is one of the least reliable ways to prevent pregnancy. On the CDC's effectiveness chart, 22 out of every 100 women whose partners use withdrawal become pregnant within the first year of typical use. Compare that with about 18 for condoms, 9 for the pill, and fewer than 1 for the implant. Withdrawal means completely removing the penis from the vagina and away from the outside genitals before ejaculation, and in real life the timing often fails. It also gives no protection at all against STIs, including HIV. Pregnancy can even happen when sperm merely contacts the vagina. If avoiding pregnancy matters to you, a condom or another modern method is a far safer choice, and clinics can help you pick one.
key_points_en: With typical use, 22 out of 100 women relying on withdrawal become pregnant within a year
Withdrawal is far less effective than condoms, the pill, or the implant
Withdrawal gives no protection against STIs, including HIV
Sperm contact with the vagina can cause pregnancy even without ejaculation inside
referral_conditions: Couples relying on withdrawal who want reliable protection should discuss modern contraceptive methods at a clinic or pharmacy
After withdrawal failure, emergency contraception can be sought within 3 to 5 days
prohibited_claims: Never describe withdrawal as a reliable contraceptive method
Never say withdrawal protects against STIs or HIV

claims.text_en: With typical use of withdrawal, 22 out of 100 women experience an unintended pregnancy within the first year.
Withdrawal is far less effective than other methods on the CDC chart: typical-use first-year pregnancy rates are 18 per 100 for male condoms, 9 per 100 for the pill, and 0.05 per 100 for the implant.
Withdrawal (coitus interruptus) does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV infection.
Withdrawal requires the penis to be completely removed from the vagina and away from the external genitalia before ejaculation.
Pregnancy can happen if sperm comes into contact with the vagina, even without penetration, although the risk this way is very low.

cards.answer_en: A late period has many possible causes, and pregnancy is only one of them. The NHS lists pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss, being overweight, and doing too much exercise as common reasons. Hormonal contraception such as the pill, the injection, or a hormonal IUS can also change or stop periods, and so can breastfeeding. Hormonal conditions matter too: polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and the start of menopause, usually between ages 45 and 55, can both stop periods. If pregnancy is possible, do a test from the first day of the missed period. See a doctor if you have missed three periods in a row, if periods have become irregular, or if a missed period comes with symptoms like weight change, tiredness, or new facial hair growth.
key_points_en: Pregnancy, stress, weight change, and heavy exercise are common causes of a late period
Hormonal contraception and breastfeeding can delay or stop periods
PCOS and perimenopause can also stop periods
Do a pregnancy test from the first day of a missed period
Three missed periods in a row is a reason to see a doctor
referral_conditions: Missed period 3 times in a row
Periods not started by age 15
Periods have become irregular
Missed period with other symptoms such as weight gain or loss, tiredness, facial hair growth, or skin changes
prohibited_claims: Never say a late period always means pregnancy
Never dismiss three or more missed periods as normal without assessment

claims.text_en: Common causes of a missed or late period include pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss, being overweight, and doing too much exercise.
Certain hormonal methods of contraception, such as the contraceptive pill, contraceptive injection or IUS, and breastfeeding can also cause missed periods.
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and the start of menopause (perimenopause), usually between ages 45 and 55, can cause periods to stop.

See a doctor if you have missed your period 3 times in a row, if periods have not started by age 15, if periods have become irregular, or if a missed period comes with symptoms like weight gain or loss, tiredness, or hair growth on the face.
Most pregnancy tests can be carried out from the first day of a missed period.

cards.answer_en: Pregnancy is possible during a window of days around ovulation, when an egg is released from the ovary. The NHS explains that in most women ovulation happens around 10 to 16 days before the next period, and someone with a regular 28-day cycle is likely to be fertile around day 14. The fertile window is wider than the day of ovulation itself, because sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to 7 days after sex, so sex in the days before ovulation can still lead to pregnancy. Timing shifts between cycles, and with early ovulation or a short cycle, pregnancy is possible soon after a period finishes. Because the fertile days are hard to predict exactly, counting days alone is a risky way to avoid pregnancy.
key_points_en: Pregnancy happens in the days around ovulation
Ovulation usually occurs around 10 to 16 days before the next period
Sperm survive up to 7 days, so sex before ovulation can cause pregnancy
In a regular 28-day cycle, fertility is likely around day 14
Cycle timing varies, so fertile days are hard to predict exactly
referral_conditions: Anyone wanting to prevent pregnancy reliably should discuss contraceptive methods with a health worker rather than relying on cycle counting
prohibited_claims: Never present fertile-window counting as a guaranteed way to avoid pregnancy
Never state exact universal safe days that apply to everyone

claims.text_en: There is only a short time in the cycle when pregnancy can occur, and that is the time around ovulation.
In most women ovulation happens around 10 to 16 days before the next period, and women with a regular 28-day cycle are likely to be fertile around day 14.
Because sperm can survive in the fallopian tubes for up to 7 days after sex, sex in the days before ovulation can result in pregnancy.
It is possible to get pregnant soon after a period finishes if ovulation is early or the menstrual cycle is short.

cards.answer_en: Yes. Most sexually transmitted infections cause no symptoms at all, so a person can have an STI, feel completely well, and still pass it to a partner. The World Health Organization reports that more than 1 million curable STIs are acquired every day worldwide among people aged 15 to 49, and the majority of these infections are asymptomatic. Even when symptoms do appear, they can be vague and easy to mistake for something else. This is why feeling fine is not proof of being infection free, and why testing matters after unprotected sex or a new partner. Signs like unusual discharge from the vagina or penis, or sores and ulcers around the genitals, should always prompt a visit to a health facility, but silence from the body is not an all-clear.
key_points_en: Most STIs cause no symptoms
More than 1 million curable STIs are acquired every day among people 15 to 49
Symptoms, when present, can be non-specific
Testing is the way to know your status, not how you feel
Discharge or genital ulcers should prompt a clinic visit
referral_conditions: Vaginal or urethral discharge, or anogenital ulcers: seek care at a health facility
Unprotected sex or a condom failure with a partner of unknown status: consider STI testing
prohibited_claims: Never say absence of symptoms means absence of infection
Never say only people with many partners get STIs

claims.text_en: The majority of curable STIs acquired worldwide are asymptomatic.
More than 1 million curable sexually transmitted infections are acquired every day worldwide in people 15 to 49 years old.
STIs are often asymptomatic, and when symptoms occur they can be non-specific.
Symptoms such as vaginal or urethral discharge and anogenital ulcers should prompt seeking care.

cards.answer_en: STI risk can be brought down a great deal with a few practical steps. The World Health Organization states that when used correctly and consistently, condoms offer one of the most effective methods of protection against STIs, and the NHS calls using a condom every time you have sex the best way to protect yourself and your partner from HIV and other STIs. Ethiopia's national guideline strongly recommends dual protection, meaning condoms used to prevent both pregnancy and infection, for anyone at risk of STIs and HIV. Safe and highly effective vaccines exist for two viral STIs, hepatitis B and HPV. Finally, if one partner is diagnosed, treating sexual partners is an important part of care, so encourage a partner to get tested and treated too.
key_points_en: Correct and consistent condom use is one of the most effective protections against STIs
Vaccines protect against hepatitis B and HPV
Ethiopia's guideline recommends dual protection with condoms for those at risk
Treating sexual partners is an important part of STI care
Testing after risk exposure helps catch silent infections
referral_conditions: Diagnosis of an STI: partners should be treated as part of case management
Symptoms such as discharge or genital ulcers: seek care at a health facility
prohibited_claims: Never say condoms remove all STI risk completely
Never suggest vaccination replaces the need for condoms or testing

claims.text_en: When used correctly and consistently, condoms offer one of the most effective methods of protection against STIs.
Safe and highly effective vaccines are available for two viral STIs: hepatitis B and HPV.
Treating sexual partners is an important component of STI case management.
Ethiopia's national family planning guideline strongly recommends dual protection for all clients suspected of STIs and HIV/AIDS.
Using a condom every time you have sex is the best way to protect you and your partner from HIV and other STIs.

cards.answer_en: HIV is not spread through everyday contact. The World Health Organization states that people cannot become infected with HIV through ordinary day-to-day contact such as kissing, hugging, shaking hands, or sharing personal objects, food, or water. So sharing a meal, a cup, a bathroom, a classroom, or a home with someone living with HIV carries no risk, and neither does a handshake or a hug. HIV is only transmitted through the exchange of certain body fluids from a person living with HIV, namely blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal secretions, and from mother to child during pregnancy and delivery. Knowing this protects people living with HIV from unfair fear and stigma, and helps everyone focus on the real routes of transmission and the real means of prevention, like condoms and treatment.
key_points_en: HIV is not spread by kissing, hugging, or shaking hands
Sharing personal objects, food, or water cannot transmit HIV
HIV spreads only through certain body fluids: blood, breast milk, semen, vaginal secretions
Everyday social contact with someone living with HIV is completely safe
referral_conditions: Possible real exposure, such as unprotected sex or blood contact: seek testing and ask a provider about post-exposure prophylaxis
prohibited_claims: Never suggest casual contact, shared food, shared utensils, or shared toilets can transmit HIV
Never use wording that stigmatises people living with HIV

claims.text_en: People cannot become infected with HIV through ordinary day-to-day contact such as kissing, hugging, shaking hands, or sharing personal objects, food or water.
HIV is transmitted via the exchange of body fluids from people living with HIV, including blood, breast milk, semen, and vaginal secretions, and from mother to child during pregnancy and delivery.

HIV prevention options include male or female condoms, medical male circumcision, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, pre-exposure prophylaxis, post-exposure prophylaxis, and antiretroviral therapy for pregnant women.

cards.answer_en: The window period is the time between HIV exposure and when a test can detect HIV in the body. During this time a test can be negative even though the person has HIV and can pass it on. The World Health Organization notes that most people develop antibodies to HIV within 28 days of infection, so antibody tests may miss a very recent infection, and anyone testing negative after a recent exposure should retest after 28 days. The CDC gives windows by test type: nucleic acid tests detect HIV 10 to 33 days after exposure, laboratory antigen/antibody tests 18 to 45 days, rapid antigen/antibody tests 18 to 90 days, and antibody self-tests 23 to 90 days. If a test after possible exposure is negative, test again once the window for that test has passed.
key_points_en: The window period is the gap between exposure and when a test can detect HIV
Most people develop HIV antibodies within 28 days of infection
Test windows range from 10 to 33 days for NAT up to 23 to 90 days for antibody self-tests
A negative test during the window period does not rule out HIV
Retest after the window period for the test you took
referral_conditions: Negative test after a recent potential exposure: retest after the window period for the test taken
Very recent potential exposure: ask a health provider urgently about post-exposure prophylaxis
prohibited_claims: Never say a negative test taken immediately after exposure proves someone does not have HIV
Never state a single universal window period for all test types

claims.text_en: The window period is the time between HIV exposure and when a test can detect HIV in the body.
In most cases people develop antibodies to HIV within 28 days of infection, and those testing negative after a recent exposure should retest after 28 days.

CDC window periods by test type are: nucleic acid test 10 to 33 days after exposure, antigen/antibody lab test 18 to 45 days, rapid antigen/antibody test 18 to 90 days, and antibody self-test 23 to 90 days.
During the window period a person can have undetectable antibody levels but may still transmit HIV.
If an HIV test after a potential exposure is negative, get tested again after the window period for the test you took.
